label: Bank statements to journal entries
description: Read a bank statement PDF, work out who each payment was to or from, classify it, and produce journal entries that provably foot. Specified by docs/backend-model-evaluation.md.

documents.describe: Seven bank statements, one per account, four currencies, six business days

passes.name: extract
prompt: You are parsing a bank statement PDF into transaction rows for a fund administrator.
Write a Python file, `parse.py`. The `kit` module gives you:
kit.page_count() -> int
kit.lines(page)  -> visual lines on that page, top to bottom.
PAGES ARE 1-BASED: iterate range(1, kit.page_count()+1).
Each line has:
line.text                  str  — the whole line
line.words                 list[dict] — each with "text" and "x0"
line.between(a, b)         str  — the text of that column,
ALREADY JOINED. Not a list.
line.words_between(a, b)   list[dict] — the words themselves
kit.column_positions() -> dict of the left edge of every column, read from
the statement's own header row:
bank_reference, customer_reference, trn_type,
value_date, credit, debit, balance, time, post_date
kit.write_result(rows) -> writes /work/result.json
Each row is a dict with these keys:
bank_reference, trn_type, value_date, post_date, time, narrative,
credit, debit, balance, account_number, currency, page
Amounts are strings, no thousands separators, sign exactly as printed. Exactly
one of credit/debit is set; the other is None. Rows in statement order, newest
first.
## What statements actually look like
- **They span several pages, and the transactions continue across them.** The
column header row repeats at the top of every page; so does the "Statement
details" block. Skip the furniture, keep the transactions, and keep them in
page order — a row dropped at a page boundary breaks the chain by exactly
the amount of that row.
- Day boundaries appear *between* transactions as "Balance as at close <date>"
and "Balance brought forward <date>". They are markers, not transactions,
and their amount sits in a different column from the transaction balances.
- The narrative is a continuation line under its transaction, labelled
`Narrative`. The bank wraps long names mid-word by inserting a comma, so
"NORDVIK INFRASTR, UCTURE V SCSP" is one name, not two.

checks.name: balance_chain
checks.describe: a row's balance minus its amount must equal the NEXT row's balance

checks.name: closing_balance
checks.describe: the first row's balance equals the closing balance printed on page 1

checks.name: printed_openings
checks.describe: every "Balance brought forward" marker must reproduce from the movements

checks.name: row_count
checks.describe: one row per transaction. "Balance as at close" and "Balance brought forward" are day markers, NOT transactions

checks.name: reference_provenance
checks.describe: every bank_reference appears literally in the PDF text

text: `line.between(a, b)` returns a **string**; `line.words_between(a, b)` returns
the word dicts. Writing `" ".join(w["text"] for w in line.between(a, b))`
iterates the characters of a string and raises TypeError — that mistake cost
two earlier runs every attempt they had.
This statement prints no "Balance brought forward" marker at all, so
`printed_openings` will come back UNRESOLVED. That is expected and does not
block acceptance — do not invent a marker to satisfy it.
`bank_reference` must appear **literally** in the PDF. Join words with a single
space where the document has one and with nothing where it does not. Two
failure shapes to avoid: a space between every character, and stripping all
spaces so the next column's text runs into the reference.

passes.name: resolve
prompt: The transaction rows have already been extracted and their arithmetic verified.
Your job is to resolve each row against the reference lists and classify it.
Write a Python file, `resolve.py`. The `kit` module gives you:
kit.rows()              -> the extracted rows, as dicts
kit.tables()            -> the names of the reference lists
t = kit.table(name)
t.columns             -> its column names
t.contains(col, v)    -> bool, exact then case-insensitive
t.find(col, v)        -> the whole row, or None
t.values(col)         -> every value in that column
t.candidates(col, v)  -> near matches, ranked
kit.write_result(rows)  -> writes /work/result.json
The lists available are:
legal_entities   Legal Entity
related_parties  Related Party
vendors          Vendor
investors        Investor
project_codes    Project Code, New Project Code
deals_positions  Deal Name, Position
Emit every input row, in the same order, with these keys added and every
original key kept unchanged:
counterparty_raw     the sender or beneficiary exactly as the narrative
writes it, or null if the narrative names none
counterparty_match   {status, matched_name, table}
project_code_raw     the project word exactly as the narrative writes it,
or null
project_code_match   {status, matched_name, table}
classification       one of the labels listed below
`status` is one of:
MATCH          you found it verbatim in a reference list. Put the list's
name in `table` and the value as that list holds it in
`matched_name`.
UNRESOLVED     you pulled a value out of the narrative and it is not in
any list. Keep `counterparty_raw`; leave `matched_name` null.
CANNOT_VERIFY  the narrative names nothing to resolve, so there was
nothing to look up.
FAIL           the row is malformed and you cannot proceed.
## How the bank writes things
- Names are truncated, capitalised, and wrapped mid-word with an inserted
comma. `NORDVIK INFRASTR, UCTURE V SCSP` is one name.
- The master lists hold the clean, cased full name. `NI ABF I SCSP` in a
narrative is `NI ABF I SCSp` in the related party list — matching is
case-insensitive, so `t.contains` will find it.
- The project word appears in the narrative, often after the word PROJECT.
## Classification
`classification` must be exactly one of these eight strings, copied verbatim.
Nothing else is accepted, and a label of your own invention fails the run:
Investment            buying or selling a position
Investment Transfer   moving money between entities for an investment
Vendor                paying a supplier
Related Party         a movement with an entity on the related party list
Investor              a capital call or distribution
Internal              a transfer between the platform's own accounts
Other                 bank charges, interest, and anything routine
Review                none of the above
Whether an investment row is equity or a loan is carried by the narrative —
shares and equity on one side, loan principal and accrued interest on the
other — but that distinction belongs in the position, not in this label.
**Classification comes from the narrative, not from whether a lookup
succeeded.** A row whose counterparty is UNRESOLVED is still classifiable: the
narrative says what kind of movement it is regardless of whether the name is on
a list. `Review` is for a row you genuinely cannot place — in this week's data
that is about three rows in a hundred, not most of them. A commission or a bank
charge is `Other`; a transfer between the platform's own accounts is `Internal`;
a loan or purchase to a named entity is `Investment` or `Investment Transfer`.
Reaching for `Review` because the counterparty did not resolve is the mistake to
avoid; a made-up label is the other one.

checks.name: provenance
checks.describe: a counterparty you claim to have pulled out must appear in that row's narrative

checks.name: membership
checks.describe: a MATCH must name a list and a value that is really in it

checks.name: completeness
checks.describe: every row carries a status for both — an omitted resolution is unexamined, not unresolved

checks.name: vocabulary
checks.describe: the classification must be one of the declared labels

text: Caution belongs in the **matching**, not in the reading. Two different jobs:
- `counterparty_raw` and `project_code_raw` are *transcription*. If the
narrative names a party or a project, copy it out — always, whether or not
any list contains it. Leaving it null claims the narrative named nobody,
which is a different and usually wrong statement, and it robs the reviewer
of the one thing they need to decide the row.
- The `_match` status is *judgement*, and there you are strict. Forcing an
unmatched name to the nearest list entry is the single worst thing you can
do here: an UNRESOLVED row goes to a person, a wrong match goes into the
accounts. Never use `candidates` to pick a match.
So a narrative naming `NI V KALVIK TOPCO LTD.` that is in no list gives
`counterparty_raw` set and status UNRESOLVED. Only a narrative that names no
party at all — a bank charge, an interest posting — gives null and
CANNOT_VERIFY. In this week's data roughly half the rows name somebody, and
about half of those resolve.
A `counterparty_raw` must be a literal substring of that row's own narrative.
Copy it out rather than reconstructing it, and if the narrative names nobody,
set it to null with status CANNOT_VERIFY.
The classification must be one of the eight strings listed above, copied
exactly. Not a variation, not a refinement, not a hyphenated pair — if the
row is an equity purchase the label is still `Investment`, and if none of
the eight fits, it is `Review`.
A MATCH has to name the list it came from and the value as that list holds
it. Use `t.find(col, v)` and read the value back out of the row it returns,
rather than echoing what the narrative said. If `find` returns None, the
status is UNRESOLVED.
